explanations.explanation: Three hundred, friend. Jashobeam son of Hachmoni, chief of the officers, wielded his spear against three hundred men and killed them at one time. I get nervous when a batch has three dozen cookies and one is crooked. Three HUNDRED men, one spear, and he just kept going.

Five hundred would be a big number, but the text says three hundred. Jashobeam, chief of the officers, wielded his spear against three hundred men, whom he killed at one time. Three hundred was already plenty. Nobody needed him to add two more hundred to impress me.

Seven hundred is a big jump from what the text says. It tells us Jashobeam wielded his spear against three hundred men and killed them at one time. I understand wanting to round up, because I do it with cookie counts all the time. Here the number stays at three hundred.

I get why you'd think so, but the text says the opposite. At the field full of barley, the troops fled from the Philistines (1 Chronicles 11:13). Holding ground didn't happen for them. They took off, and it was Eleazar and David who stayed.

That's right, the troops fled. The Philistines gathered at Pas-dammim for battle, and at a field full of barley the troops ran from them (1 Chronicles 11:13). When I hear a battle is coming, I'm the first one under the counter. So I can't judge those troops one bit.

explanations.answer: Stand in the middle of the field and defend it
explanations.explanation: Yes, right in the middle. While the troops fled, Eleazar and David stationed themselves in the middle of the field and defended it. They struck down the Philistines too. Two men in the middle of a field while everybody else leaves. That's a lot of nerve.

explanations.answer: Chase after the troops to bring them back
explanations.explanation: The text never has them chasing anybody. It says Eleazar and David stationed themselves in the middle of the field and defended it. They stayed put while the troops fled. Picture two men planted in a field while everybody else is running past them.

explanations.answer: Set fire to the barley and slip away
explanations.explanation: No fire and no slipping away here. Eleazar and David stationed themselves in the middle of the field and defended it. Setting it on fire would be the opposite of defending it. They struck down the Philistines, and the LORD brought about a great victory.

The LORD, friend. Eleazar and David struck down the Philistines, and the text says, "…the LORD brought about a great victory." The two men did the fighting, and the credit for the victory goes to the LORD. That's worth remembering whenever you finish something big.

An army sounds reasonable, but the troops had fled from that field (1 Chronicles 11:13). The text says Eleazar and David struck down the Philistines and "…the LORD brought about a great victory." So it wasn't a big army doing the work, and it wasn't anybody else either.

No priest shows up in this scene. Eleazar and David struck down the Philistines, and "…the LORD brought about a great victory." The text gives the victory to the LORD. It doesn't give it to a person, and that includes people holding a title.

Bethlehem it is. David said, "Oh, that someone would get me a drink of water from the well near the gate of Bethlehem!" The text says the garrison of the Philistines was at Bethlehem at that time. Of all the wells to wish for, he picked one in a town with a Philistine garrison.

Hebron is a real place, but it's not the one David named. He said, "Oh, that someone would get me a drink of water from the well near the gate of Bethlehem!" The text says the garrison of the Philistines was at Bethlehem at that time. So Bethlehem is the town to remember.

Jericho isn't in this story at all. David longed for water from "…the well near the gate of Bethlehem!" The text says the garrison of the Philistines was at Bethlehem at that time. So the town to remember is Bethlehem.

explanations.answer: He pours it out to the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's what David did. The Three broke through a Philistine camp to bring him water, and he refused to drink it. Instead, he poured it out to the LORD. I think that tells us how much those men's gift meant to him.

That would be the obvious move, since he'd longed for that water. But the text says David refused to drink it. Instead, he poured it out to the LORD. After all that trouble to bring it, he never took a sip.

explanations.answer: He gives it to the troops
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about the troops getting it. It says David refused to drink the water, and instead he poured it out to the LORD. He said the Three had brought it at the risk of their lives (1 Chronicles 11:19). That's where the water went: out to the LORD.

True, and David says it himself. He says, "How can I drink the blood of these men who risked their lives?" The text adds that because they had brought it at the risk of their lives, David refused to drink it. A water run turned into a risk of lives, and he treated it that way.

This one is true, and the text says why. David said, "How can I drink the blood of these men who risked their lives?" Because they had brought it at the risk of their lives, he refused to drink it. The reason is right there in the verse, so no guessing is needed.

It's a close call, but the text says otherwise. Abishai, brother of Joab, became the Three's commander "…even though he was not included among the Three." He won a name along with them and was doubly honored. But he never got a spot in the Three.

That's right. Abishai was doubly honored above the Three and became their commander, "…even though he was not included among the Three." He's the boss of a team he isn't officially on. If that happened at my bakery, I'd need a minute to understand the org chart.

Moab, friend. Benaiah son of Jehoiada, a man of valor from Kabzeel, struck down two champions of Moab. The text calls him a man of many exploits, and this is one of them. On a snowy day he also went down into a pit and killed a lion.
Edom isn't the nation the text names. It says Benaiah struck down two champions of Moab. The verse is clear that these two champions came from Moab. Hold on to Moab for this one.

Ammon does show up in this list, because Zelek the Ammonite is one of the mighty men (1 Chronicles 11:39). But the two champions Benaiah struck down were from Moab, not Ammon. A name in the list can easily tag along into a different story. Keep Moab for Benaiah's champions.

explanations.answer: He goes down into the pit and kills it
explanations.explanation: He went down into the pit and killed it, and the text says it was a snowy day. Most people see a lion in a pit and stay on the top side, very politely. Benaiah went down. The text calls him a man of valor and a man of many exploits.

explanations.answer: He covers the pit and leaves it there
explanations.explanation: That's a sensible plan, but it's not what the text says. On a snowy day, Benaiah went down into a pit and killed a lion. The text has him going in after it.

explanations.answer: He waits for it to climb out first
explanations.explanation: Waiting for the lion to come up would be one way to do it, but that's not what the text says. On a snowy day, Benaiah went down into a pit and killed a lion. The text has him going down to it.

explanations.answer: He snatches the spear and kills him with it
explanations.explanation: Exactly. The Egyptian's spear was like a weaver's beam, but Benaiah went against him with a club, snatched the spear from his hand, and killed the Egyptian with his own spear. The text says the Egyptian was a huge man, five cubits tall. I'd say a club against that spear is a bold way to show up.

explanations.answer: He knocks the spear away and the Egyptian runs
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't have the Egyptian running anywhere. Benaiah snatched the spear from his hand and killed the Egyptian with his own spear. So the Egyptian didn't get away, and the spear didn't just land on the ground. Benaiah took it and used it.

explanations.answer: He calls the Three to fight beside him
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention any helpers in this scene. It says Benaiah went against the huge Egyptian, who had a spear like a weaver's beam, with a club. Then he snatched the spear from the Egyptian's hand and killed him with it. It also says Benaiah did not become one of the Three (1 Chronicles 11:25).

True. The text says Benaiah "…was most honored among the Thirty, but he did not become one of the Three." Out of the whole group of Thirty, nobody beat him on honor. He still didn't reach the Three, which is a funny spot to be in.

The text says it the other way. Benaiah "…was most honored among the Thirty, but he did not become one of the Three." So among the Thirty, nobody had more honor than him. It's a big honor even without that spot in the Three.

Guard is right. Benaiah did not become one of the Three, but the text says David appointed him over his guard. It also says he was most honored among the Thirty. The text puts those two facts side by side.
Vineyards are never mentioned in this passage. The text says David appointed Benaiah over his guard. That's the job the verse names, and it's the one to remember.
A treasury is a big job, but it isn't mentioned in this passage. The text says David appointed Benaiah over his guard. Guard is the job the verse gives him.
